summary: "Greeta ja hänen Herransa" by Arvid Järnefelt is a novel written in the early 20th century. It portrays a devout, insular Swedish-speaking farming family that flees village gossip and rebuilds a secluded life in the Finnish backwoods. Centering on Greeta’s steadfast faith and her son Helge’s quiet leadership, the story explores isolation versus the encroaching modern world, along with duty, work, and desire. The opening of the novel follows taciturn Anders, who marries his cousin Greeta and moves far from their Uusimaa village to escape meddling and live by strict Old Testament habits. He fashions a stony, beautiful homestead; after years, children arrive, and only son Helge grows into a skilled, reserved craftsman. When Anders dies, the family learns their tenure gives them no right to remain, but Helge assumes command: he revives the household’s scripture reading, negotiates with the new owner, uses hidden savings, buys a plot in a birch grove, and moves the buildings. As factories, sawmills, and summer villas creep near, Helge keeps to his craft and skepticism, deciding to build a boat and secretly hauling planks by moonlight. On this night ride he glimpses a friend in a compromising tryst, and two lively servant girls, Fluura and Maija, hop onto his wagon; the scene closes with Maija pressed close beside him as they roll into the dark.
